doc.title: Al Tinney interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Learning on the job from Don Byas and Teddy Wilson
summary: Byas pushed him through all keys; his schooling came from musicians, and Wilson became a friend.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well it must have been quite a challenge working with guys like Don Byas and so forth?

Oh man. Don Byas. One night he took a tune, and I’m glad I knew the tune, and he said, “Let’s go through the keys, Al.” I said, “Oh no.” He said, “Come on, man, you can—” I said, “I don’t even know it in this key.” But we went through all of the keys. And this is where I got all my schooling, from these guys. Him and another trumpet player, I forget his name now, but these guys were all my teachers. Not just one person, I had several teachers you know. I learned from several people.
And it wasn’t even like official lessons, it was just like on the job, right?

Oh no, it was just — here’s how you do this Al. And I would do it like that. Because like I used to love Teddy Wilson and I used to actually start playing similar to him. And then him and I became very good friends and I would go up to his house to get the data for an orchestration that I was going to do for him and his small group down at — what is it called, it was — well anyhow, he was in the bathroom shaving or something and I was playing the piano and he sticks his head out and he says, “You’ve been listening to Tatum, ey?” I said, “Oh no, no, no, I’m still a Wilson —” because I had been listening to Tatum.
